2. Brief facts of the case are that respondent had given a friendly loan of Rs. 30,00,000/- to the appellant in in May, 2016 for a period of six months.

3. Ld. counsel for appellant argued that the impugned order is not sustainable in the eyes of law as the same is based on perverse and ill presumptions.
The impugned order is arbitrary, illegal and contrary to the principles of natural justice and not based upon the correct appreciation of evidence and documents on record.

However, no presumptions had arised in favour of the respondent/
complainant.
It has been further argued that Ld. Trial court had failed to consider the financial capacity of the respondent/ complainant as to how he was able to give huge amount of Rs. 30 lacs to the appellant.
The accused/appellant was able to established a probable defence which was not considered by the Ld. Trial Court.
It has been further argued that no receipt qua payment of cash amount/ loan of Rs. 30 lacs has been placed on record.
The complainant/ respondent has not examined any independent witness in whose presence the alleged loan was advanced to the appellant.
There was no legally enforceable debt was due against the appellant in which discharge the cheque in question was issued.
The complainant/ respondent had also not placed on record the his bank account statement to show whether he was having the said amount to advance as loan.

The accused/petitioner has established a probable defence by creating a probable doubt and onus was on the complainant/respondent to prove the adequate doubts to which complainant have miserably failed.

4. It has been further argued that it was admitted by complainant that he was not in a financial condition to grant loan and there is grave suspicion on the financial capacity of the complainant and that during his cross examination CW-1 deposed different facts to the same which were mentioned by her in her complaint.
Therefore, the respondent has failed to prove the basic ingredients of the offence u/s 138 NI Act.

6. I have gone through the Trial Court record and have given thoughtful consideration to the rival submissions made on behalf of the parties.
7. To rebut the presumption u/s 139 NI Act, accused can lead direct evidence or can rely on the materials submitted by the complainant in order to raise a probable defence.
The inference of preponderance of probabilities can also be drawn by reference to the circumstances upon which the accused relied upon.

In case titled Basalingappa Vs. Mudibasappa (2019) 5 SCC 418, decided on April 9, 2019, The Hon'ble Supreme Court of India has held as follows:
"25.
We have noticed the ratio laid down by this Court in the above cases on Sections 118(a) and 139, we now summarize the principles enumerated by this court in following manner:

sentences.text: 25.1 Once the execution of cheque is admitted Section 139 of the Act mandates a presumption that the cheque was for the discharge of any debt or other liability.
25.2 The presumption under Section 139 is a rebuttable presumption and the onus is on the accused to raise the probable defence.
The standard of proof for rebutting the presumption is that of preponderance of probabilities.

25.3 To rebut the presumption, it is open for the accused to rely on evidence led by him or the accused can also rely on the materials submitted by the complainant in order to raise a probable defence.
Inference of preponderance of probabilities can be drawn not only from the materials brought on record by the parties but also by reference to the circumstances upon which they rely.
25.4 That it is not necessary for the accused to come in the witness box in support of his defence, Section 139 imposed an evidentiary burden and not a persuasive burden.
25.5 It is not necessary for the accused to come in the witness box to support his defence.

8. In this case, the main contention of the appellant is that he had not taken loan of Rs. 30 Lacs as alleged by the respondent nor the cheque in question was issued to respondent rather it was issued to one Narender who was his partner in business and cousin of the respondent.
Ld. Counsel for appellant has also raised question on the financial capacity of respondent/ complainant.
To prove this defence, he has relied upon the evidence led by him as alleged cross examination of respondent.

9. Before appreciation of evidence of the present case, this court would like to refer to the case law on the aspect of financial capacity of the complainant to grant a friendly loan and legal enforceable debt.

In the Judgment of the case titled as "Kulvinder Singh Vs. Kafeel Ahmed", 2014 (2) JCC (NI)
100, it was observed that:
"The case of the petitioner is nutshell is that he had been approached by the respondent and he had advanced a loan of Rs.9,30,000/ in the first instance.

entities.text:
Kulvinder Singh Vs. Kafeel Ahmed", 2014 (2) JCC (NI)
100
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: If such a huge amount of money is advanced as a loan to the respondent, the petitioner ought to have shown to the court concerned as to the source from where he had generated such a huge amount.
In his examination/cross examination, he stated that he had sold his machinery but he failed to produce any record to that effect.
He has not reflected the loan advanced to the respondent in his income tax return not is he able to tell to the court the Ward in which the income tax return is filed.

The learned Magistrate has rightly placed reliance on the provisions of Section 269 SS of Income Tax Act where in it is specifically laid down that if a loan is advanced which is more than Rs.20,000/, it has to be by way of writing reflected in the books of account but nothing of that sort has been done in the instant case.
Obviously, this clearly creates a doubt regarding the truthfulness of the stand taken by the petitioner that he had advanced a loan of Rs.9,30,000/ to the respondent."

10. In the Judgment of the case tilted as "G. Pankajakshmi Amma and Ors. Vs. Mathai Mathew",
(2004) 12 SCC 83, it was so observed that:

sentences.text: There is any reason also why the impugned Judgment cannot be upheld.
According to the 1st respondent these transactions were to be unaccounted transactions.
According to the 1st respondent, all these amounts are paid in cash.
If these are unaccounted transactions then they are illegal transactions.
No court can come to the aid of the party in an illegal transaction.
It is settled law that in such cases the loss must be allowed to lie where it falls.
In this case as these are unaccounted transaction, the court could not have lent its hands and passed a decree.

For these reasons also the suit was required to be dismissed."
11.

In Basalingappa Vs. Mudibasappa (supra), the Hon'ble Apex Court of India has observed that once the financial capacity of a lender has been questioned, it is incumbent upon him to explain his financial capacity and held as follow:-
" 29.

Thus, there is a contradiction in what was initially stated by the complainant in the complaint and in his examination-in-chief regarding date on which loan was given on one side and what was said in cross-examination in other side, which has not been satisfactorily explained.
The High Court was unduly influenced by the fact that the accused did not reply the notice denying the execution of cheque or legal liability.
Even before the trial court, appellant- accused has not denied his signature on the cheque.

30. We are of the view that when evidence was led before the Court to indicate that apart from loan of Rs.6 lakhs given to the accused, within 02 years, amount of Rs.18 lakhs have been given out by the complainant and his financial capacity being questioned, it was incumbent on the complainant to have explained his financial capacity.
Court cannot insist on a person to lead negative evidence.
The observation of the High Court that trial court's finding that the complainant failed to prove his financial capacity of lending money is perverse cannot be supported.
We fail to see that how the trial court's findings can be termed as perverse by the High Court when it was based on consideration of the evidence, which was led on behalf of the defence.

31. This Court had occasion to consider the expression "perverse" in Gamini Bala Koteswara Rao and others Vs. State of Andhra Pradesh through Secretary, (2009) 10 SCC 636, this Court held that although High Court can reappraise the evidence and conclusions drawn by the trial court but judgment of acquittal can be interfered with only judgment is against the weight of evidence.

entities.text: Gamini Bala Koteswara Rao and others Vs. State of Andhra Pradesh through Secretary, (2009) 10 SCC 636
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: In Paragraph No.14 following has been held:-
"14. We have considered the arguments advanced and heard the matter at great length.
It is true, as contended by Mr Rao, that interference in an appeal against an acquittal recorded by the trial court should be rare and in exceptional circumstances.

It is, however, well settled by now that it is open to the High Court to reappraise the evidence and conclusions drawn by the trial court but only in a case when the judgment of the trial court is stated to be perverse.

The word "perverse" in terms as Sunil Kumar Ahlawat vs Manoj Kumar on 12 November, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/59725940/
5 understood in law has been defined to mean "against the weight of evidence".

entities.text: Sunil Kumar Ahlawat vs Manoj Kumar on 12 November, 2024 Indian Kanoon
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: We have to see accordingly as to whether the judgment of the trial court which has been found perverse by the High Court was in fact so."
32. The High Court without discarding the evidence, which was led by defence could not have held that finding of trial court regarding financial capacity of the complainant is perverse.

We are, thus,
satisfied that accused has raised a probable defence and the findings of the trial court that complainant failed to prove his financial capacity are based on evidence led by the defence.
The observations of the High Court that findings of the trial court are perverse are unsustainable.

We,
thus, are of the view that judgment of the High Court is unsustainable."
12. In the present case, the respondent is silent about the source of funds of loan amount of Rs. 30 lacs in his complaint and evidence by way of affidavit.
In his cross examination conducted on 07.12.2017, respondent deposed that he earned Rs. Four lacs per annum in the last 2& 1/2- 3 years by way of agriculture.

In his cross-examination conducted on 26.06.2019, respondent deposed that when loan was given, he used to earn around Rs. Four lacs yearly out of which his expenditure was around 1-1.5 lacs and he used to save the rest.
No ITR or any other document has been produced by the respondent to prove his annual income.
A person with annual savings of Rs. 2.5 lacs for 3-4 years is not financially capable to grant loan of Rs. 30 lacs.
Respondent had deposed that a amount was received by him in his father's land is mentioned in his passbook.
The money was received by his father from government on acquisition in his bank account and the same was transferred by his father into his bank account.
Admittedly, no statement of bank account has been produced by the respondent to prove the transfer of funds by his father in bank account.
Nor it is the case of the respondent that he had withdrawn the loan of Rs. 30 lacs from his bank account before handing over the same to appellant.
The respondent has failed to disclosed the source of the funds of huge amount of loan of Rs. 30 lacs.
If, the respondent was having sufficient funds in his bank account then why he had gave the loan amount to appellant in cash instead of bank transaction/ cheque.
13. Admittedly, no document in respect of alleged loan was prepared between him and appellant/accused.
In his evidence by way of affidavit, respondent had stated that keeping in view the friendly relations, he had given loan of Rs. 30 lacs to appellant at his residence.
Whereas in his cross examination he had deposed that the loan amount was given in presence of his father and husband of his bua's daughter I.e. Sanjay at home of the respondent.
Thus, there is contradiction whether the loan amount is given at the residence of appellant or at the residence of respondent.
The respondent has not examined the persons in whose presence the alleged payment was made to appellant.
14. To controvert the stand of respondent, the appellant examined himself and Sh. Vicky.
Appellant deposed that he know the respondent through his cousin Narender Pal Mudgil as they both were working as a partner in liquor shop.
Narender Pal Mudgil looked after his bank work and has blank signed cheque book in his possession.
Narender Pal died in September, 2015.
He also deposed that he did not take any loan from respondent.
He stood the test of cross examination.
Moreover, these facts qua acquaintance of Narender Pal with appellant had been admitted by respondent in his cross examination.

6 15.

entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: The respondent must be more diligent while granting loan to the appellant without interest without any execution of documents.
If there was sufficient funds were available with the respondent then why they did not give the loan to the appellant through cheque or by bank transaction.
All these facts and circumstances belied the story of respondent.
The story of the respondent can not be relied upon especially in the absence of any documentary evidence with regard to the loan transaction of Rs. 30 lacs and his financial capacity.
16 . Moreover, the said amount was unaccounted money and it was not a legally recoverable debt.
It was held in case titled as G. Pankajakshi Amma case (supra) that if these are unaccounted transactions then they are illegal transactions.
No court can come to the aid of the party in an illegal transaction.
The respondent failed to disclose the legal source of the said loan amount.

Hence,
respondent has miserably failed to prove the fact that there is a legally recoverable debt payable by the appellant.

17. The case of the respondent has been very inconsistent and the respondent had floundered, as the cross-examination progressed and from this it can be safely concluded that the respondent has proved himself to be unreliable witness and this has made way for the appellant to prove the non existence of any loan/ consideration; or at least that it was improbable or doubtful.

These contradictions and admissions in the testimony of the respondent compelled to believe the defence raised by the appellant probable that he had not taken loan loan of Rs. 30 lacs from the respondent.

Conclusion:
18.

In view of the aforesaid discussion, the court is of the considered opinion that appellant is able to adduce a probable defence in his favour and successfully rebut the presumption u/s 139 of Negotiable Instruments Act.
The onus to prove the legal liability of the appellant shifts back to the respondent, which he has failed to discharge.
Therefore, the judgment dated 27.01.2024 and order on sentence dated 23.02.2024 can not sustain and are set aside.
Appellant is acquitted for the offence U/s 138 NI Act and is set free.
Accordingly, the appeal is allowed.
Copy of order be sent to the Ld. Trial Court alongwith TCR.
